Legion
LEE-jun
noun (a multitude of demons)
From the Latin legio, a Roman army division of some six thousand men, taken up into the Greek of the Gospels as the self-given name of the unclean spirits that possessed the Gadarene.

See also: Legion

📖 Biblical Definition

Legion is the name the unclean spirits gave themselves when our Lord demanded it of the demoniac among the tombs of the country of the Gadarenes (or Gergesenes). The man dwelt in the tombs, exceeding fierce, breaking chains and fetters, crying night and day and cutting himself with stones, an image of the ruin sin and Satan work upon the image-bearer. When Jesus came, the spirits cried out, owning Him as Son of the most high God, and besought Him not to torment them before the time. Asked his name, the man answered, “My name is Legion: for we are many”—a confession that a multitude of devils, numerous as a Roman legion, held one soul in bondage. The demons begged leave to enter the herd of swine, and our Lord granted it; the unclean spirits drove the unclean beasts, about two thousand, violently down the steep into the sea, where they were choked. The townsfolk, finding the man clothed and in his right mind, sitting at the feet of Jesus, were more afraid of the Deliverer than of the demoniac and begged Him to depart. Legion is the dictionary's standing proof of the reality, the malice, and the multitude of the powers of darkness, and of the absolute authority of Christ over them: a word from Him empties a soul that all the chains of men could not bind, for the strong man is bound by the Stronger.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The name given by the unclean spirits possessing the Gadarene demoniac, signifying their multitude; their expulsion into the swine displays the reality of the demonic and the absolute authority of Christ over the powers of darkness.

expand to see more

LEGION, noun. [Latin, legio, a Roman military division of about six thousand.] A great multitude.

In the Gospels, the self-given name of the demons possessing the man among the tombs of the Gadarenes, “for we are many.”

The man was fierce and untameable, breaking every chain, until Christ commanded the spirits to come out.

The demons entered a herd of swine, which ran down a steep place into the sea and perished.

The delivered man was found clothed and in his right mind, sitting at the feet of Jesus.

📖 Key Scripture

Mr 5:9 — "And he asked him, What is thy name? And he answered, saying, My name is Legion: for we are many."

Mr 5:13 — "And forthwith Jesus gave them leave. And the unclean spirits went out, and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea, (they were about two thousand;) and were choked in the sea."

Lu 8:30 — "And Jesus asked him, saying, What is thy name? And he said, Legion: because many devils were entered into him."

Lu 8:35 — "Then they went out to see what was done; and came to Jesus, and found the man, out of whom the devils were departed, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The modern temptation is to demythologize Legion into a case of mental illness, denying the personal reality of demons and the unique authority of Christ over them.

expand to see more

The dominant academic reading reduces the demoniac to a sufferer of psychiatric disease and the swine to folklore, treating the demons as a primitive idiom for affliction. The dictionary rejects this on the authority of the text and of the Lord, who addressed the spirits as persons, received their answer, and granted their request to enter the swine. The drowning of two thousand beasts is not a symptom of one man's mind; it is an external, witnessed event that confirms the spirits were real, many, and now expelled. To demythologize Legion is to demythologize the Christ who cast them out.

Yet the dictionary distinguishes, as Scripture does, between demonic possession and the ordinary afflictions of body and soul. Not every torment is a devil, and the rise of an enthusiastic deliverance-ministry culture that finds a demon behind every sorrow is its own corruption, often kin to the hyper-charismatic excess the confession warns against. The sober ground is this: the powers of darkness are real and malicious, the Lord Jesus is sovereign over them, and the believer's safety is not in technique but in the authority of Christ, before whom a legion flees at a word.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Latin legio, the largest unit of the Roman army; the demons borrow the soldier's word to confess their multitude and their martial hostility against the soul of man.

expand to see more

Legio, Latin, a Roman legion of roughly six thousand foot with cavalry and auxiliaries.

Legeon, the Greek transliteration found in Mark and Luke.

The term confesses both number (“we are many”) and organized hostility, as of an army arrayed against a man.

Akathartos, Greek, unclean, the standing adjective for these spirits in the Gospels.

The swine, themselves unclean beasts under the law, fittingly receive the unclean spirits cast out.

Usage

"The pastor preached Legion to show that no chain of human strength can bind a soul that a word of Christ sets free."

"He warned against both the modern denial of demons and the credulous habit of seeing one behind every trouble."

"She saw in the man clothed and in his right mind the whole work of grace: the sinner seated at the feet of Jesus."
